title: Democratic Congress Puts AI Spending and Chip Export Controls Under New Scrutiny
excerpt: With Democrats back in control of Congress, analysts expect tighter scrutiny of AI chip exports to China, new cost rules for large data centres, and investigations into the tariff and investment deals of the Trump administration.
body:
• Democrats have regained control of Congress in the midterm elections, shifting technology policy from legislation-writing to oversight: hearings, document requests and investigations.
  • Chip export controls are expected to tighten further under either party: Senate defence bill amendments would add congressional review of advanced AI chip exports, location tracking on exported chips, and a ban on selling chipmaking equipment to China under the proposed MATCH Act.
  • AI data centres face a cost fight: the proposed GRID Savings Act would make large data centres bear the full cost of expanding the power grid, and permits for Nvidia H200 exports to China allowed under the Trump administration are expected to face congressional scrutiny.
  • For investors: analysts quoted before the election warned that a Democratic sweep raises regulatory risk for AI, crypto and banking names, and one Asia portfolio manager warned any threat to the AI trade could trigger another sell-off in South Korean, Japanese and, to a lesser extent, Chinese equities.

The midterm result has changed who holds the gavels in Washington, and the technology industry is first in line for the new oversight. With the Democratic Party regaining control of Congress, the tariffs and China regulations of the Trump administration, and the investment pledges it extracted from allies, are under increased scrutiny, according to Aju Press, a South Korean business newspaper reporting on the reaction in Seoul. US political sources told the paper that Democrats plan to challenge the trade law that served as the basis for President Trump tariffs, and to investigate the allocation of the hundreds of billions of dollars in US investments promised by South Korea and Japan.

Why the power shift stops at oversight

There are hard limits on what the new Congress can reverse. Tariffs and export controls run through the executive powers of the president, and overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both the House and the Senate. The realistic channel of influence is therefore oversight: committee hearings, data requests and investigations that can slow approvals and raise the political cost of existing policy. Barron’s, writing before the election, made the same point: committee chairs can demand briefings and documents from agencies and companies, and incoming chairs have already demanded briefings from major banks on AI-related concerns.

Chips: the bipartisan exception

On China and semiconductors, the direction of travel does not depend on the election result. Both parties treat semiconductors and AI as national security issues, and regulations targeting China are expected to intensify, Aju Press reported. Renee Buck, chief executive of BCI Global, predicted in an October 30 commentary that if Democrats controlled both chambers, US-China relations would worsen and chip export controls would tighten further. In the Senate, amendments to the National Defense Authorization Act would require congressional review of advanced AI chip exports, mandate location-tracking devices on exported chips, and, through the proposed MATCH Act, prohibit the sale of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China. Export permits for Nvidia H200 chips to China, allowed under the Trump administration, are expected to come under scrutiny in hearings.

Asia carries much of the exposure. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the Korean memory makers embedded in the AI supply chain, lost their validated end-user status at the end of last year, and China one-year postponement of expanded rare earth export controls expires on November 10, Aju Press noted. Rayliant Global Advisors portfolio manager Phillip Wool warned before the result that any threat to AI could significantly affect sentiment toward equities in South Korea, Japan and, to a lesser extent, China.

Data centres: the power bill becomes the policy

The second front is electricity. Roughly $800 billion of AI data centre investment by companies including Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft runs directly into local politics over power costs, Aju Press reported. The Democrat-proposed GRID Savings Act would mandate that large data centres bear the full cost of expanding the power grid, and New York halted new permits for data centres consuming over 50 megawatts for up to a year last July. The concern is bipartisan: Barron’s noted that senators from both parties have proposed forcing data-centre developers to provide their own power, and a similar bill passed the House in September. If model development is delayed or data centre construction postponed, orders for AI accelerators fall with it — which is why a congressional oversight story is, for chip investors, also an earnings story.
